transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we can see folks coming in. quick intro, i'm maya chen, AE at Redwood Inference.
[00:08] David Park: hi Maya, David here. thanks. we were hoping to get through auth setup and a short hands-on of the TypeScript example.
[00:14] Maya Chen: perfect. Luca, do you want to kick off on the SDK quickstart and console bits? i'll cover pricing and pilot scope at the end.
[00:22] Luca Romero: yeah sure, give me a sec. ok so i'll share my screen — i'm on the Redwood console. for the SDK we have Python and TypeScript packages, pip install redwood-inference, npm i @redwood/inference, that sort of thing. the repo linked in the invite has sandbox examples.
[00:40] Priya Nair: quick note on security — we need KMS integration and keys in customer-owned KMS, we can't have plaintext keys in the console.
[00:46] Luca Romero: absolutely, we have KMS/HSM integrations. for Private deployments we can wire to your KMS and the console stores only references not raw keys — though the walkthrough will show token rotation and recommended env var patterns.
[01:01] Aisha Khan: timeline wise, if we run a pilot how long to get a dedicated pool? we have strict PII policies.
[01:07] Maya Chen: good Q. Dedicated pools can be reserved in as little as two weeks with approved contracts, but depends on region and capacity. for PII, Private deployment (VPC/on-prem) is what most banks use.
[01:18] Luca Romero: back to SDK — showing the TypeScript example. so in src/index.ts we pull in client = new Redwood({apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY}); note the env var naming, we recommend vault or secrets-manager rather than .env in prod.
[01:36] David Park: uh there's a note in our infra that we use GCP workload identity, do you have a guide for that? we prefer not to store long-lived secrets.
[01:42] Luca Romero: yes, we have a GCP workload-identity doc in the repo — it shows how to exchange tokens for short-lived credentials and attach to the service account used by the sandbox. i'll paste link in the follow-up chat.
[01:55] Maya Chen: also, for Dedicated we support short-lived tokens and can integrate with workload identity for the control plane, plus audit logs for every request at token level.
[02:06] Sam Ortiz: curious about latency and batching — our core use is real-time recommendations, ~150ms p95 target. how does batching affect that?
[02:14] Luca Romero: great question. Optimize suggests batch sizes based on observed latencies and tail behavior; you can pin a low-latency SLO which prefers smaller batches. the console gives cost vs latency trade-offs and recommended config.
[02:30] David Park: any prebuilt metrics for cost per 1k tokens for say 8k-context models?
[02:36] Maya Chen: we have benchmark sheets, but rough ballpark: hosted API cheaper for bursty dev traffic, Dedicated lowers unit cost for sustained throughput. i'll attach the benchmark spreadsheet.
[02:48] Priya Nair: how about auditability — SSO, SAML, RBAC? we require SAML OKTA and fine-grained roles.
[02:56] Luca Romero: yes, enterprise tenants get SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC. console has per-route role controls and token-scoped permissions.
[03:08] Maya Chen: let's do a quick live demo of the TypeScript quickstart. Luca, pls switch to the code sandbox.
[03:13] Luca Romero: (screen) ok here's the sample app — walkthrough: set REDWOOD_API_KEY, run npm run dev, call the generate endpoint. note the SDK auto-retries and streaming support.
[03:28] (sound of keyboard) 
[03:30] David Park: the streaming's important — we do partial renders in our UI.
[03:33] Luca Romero: right, the SDK exposes a stream interface — you can also use the streaming websocket for lower latency in some regions.
[03:43] Maya Chen: small aside, for VPC/private deployments we can route traffic over an internal endpoint so streaming still works and stays inside your network.
[03:53] Aisha Khan: i want to make sure we don't lose context. how does KV cache and prefix caching work with sessions? we're doing chat like history.
[04:01] Luca Romero: we support KV cache management and prefix caching — you can pin session caches to a dedicated instance to avoid cross-tenant leakage. cache invalidation is also exposed via API.
[04:12] Sam Ortiz: can we run a benchmark with our dataset and latency targets? we'd like to compare quantized variants.
[04:19] Luca Romero: yes, that's exactly what the Optimize playbook helps with — suggest quantization profiles and kernel selection. we can run a pilot benchmark on Dedicated and a hosted control.
[04:30] David Park: good. about auth flows, can you show the rotate key example and how to use KMS references rather than env vars? last time i saw env vars in a sample.
[04:38] Luca Romero: sure — in the repo there's a 'rotate_keys.sh' sample. for KMS-backed tokens the client reads a short token from the metadata server or secrets manager. i'll highlight the code in a sec.
[04:52] (luca scrolls) 
[04:55] Priya Nair: small transcription note: 'redwood' sometimes shows up as 'red wood' in our automatic logs, just FYI. but that's minor.
[05:02] Maya Chen: haha, yeah fireflies does that sometimes. ok next, quick look at the Console Optimize tab — this is where we recommend batching and show token level costs.
[05:12] Luca Romero: (screen) the Optimize tab has three sections: model suggestions, batching rules, and cache profiles. you can run a simulated workload to see estimated token cost savings.
[05:24] David Park: curious about model rollouts — if we push a change, can we canary to a subset of users?
[05:29] Luca Romero: yes, rollouts support canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if latency spikes or quality drops. everything's routable by policy.
[05:39] Aisha Khan: any limitations in the TypeScript SDK vs Python? one of our teams prefers Node for realtime.
[05:45] Luca Romero: feature parity is pretty high; Python has early GA for some advanced tracing hooks but Node supports streaming, function-calling, and embeddings. we'll add any missing hooks based on your feedback.
[05:58] Sam Ortiz: do you have an example of embedding generation and storage pattern? we use FAISS internally.
[06:05] Luca Romero: yes, sample shows fetching embeddings and pushing to your vector DB — we don't host vectors by default for Private/Dedicated deployments, but for hosted we offer optional vector store as a managed add-on.
[06:16] David Park: (murmur) can we talk about network egress costs in the benchmark? we run in multi-region.
[06:21] Maya Chen: definite yes. we'll capture region and egress estimates in the pilot pricing. also, we'll need to know your retention and logging retention needs for compliance.
[06:31] Aisha Khan: team question — do we need an NDA for SOC2 artifacts? security already requested vendor SOC2 before pilot.
[06:38] Maya Chen: we can do an NDA, but SOC2 report access can be handled via a secure portal. i'll have our legal/security team reach out.
[06:45] Priya Nair: please include log redaction guidance; we cannot send full PII to third-party logs.
[06:49] Luca Romero: we have log redaction patterns and mask helpers in the SDK; it's in the security checklist i'll share.
[07:00] (brief pause) 
[07:05] Maya Chen: ok practical next steps: i'll email pricing and the KMS checklist, Luca will push the TypeScript sandbox to the shared repo with a GCP workload identity example, and David will confirm SOC2 contact and PII redaction policy.
[07:20] David Park: sounds good.
[07:22] Aisha Khan: one more: can we get a timeline for Private deployment? estimated lead times?
[07:27] Maya Chen: typical Private lead time is 4–6 weeks after contract and infra prep, but we can accelerate for security-heavy customers.
[07:35] Sam Ortiz: for the pilot, can we start with hosted Dedicated and move to Private if needed?
[07:40] Luca Romero: yes that's the common path — start Dedicated for speed and cost predictability, then migrate to Private if network or data residency rules require it.
[07:50] Maya Chen: i'll put a proposed kickoff for the pilot in the follow-up — targeting week of 10/27 as discussed.
[07:56] (unintelligible, crosstalk) 
[08:02] Priya Nair: can you also share support SLAs and escalation contacts? we require 24/7 for production.
[08:08] Maya Chen: yes, enterprise SLAs and support matrix will be included in the doc pack. ok any final questions?
[08:15] David Park: none here, thanks.
[08:17] Aisha Khan: thanks everyone.
[08:20] Maya Chen: great thanks all, we'll follow up with links and the repo. bye.
[08:25] Call ends

Note: transcription contains small errors and some speaker attribution may be approximate. timestamps are approximate and sampled more frequently in the first 8 minutes for clarity; full call length was 47 minutes.
